'''Dorothy May Skinner''' (May 22, 1930 - February 12, 2005) was an [[carcinologist]], and is known for her contributions in crustacean biology. She was a research scientist at [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]].

== Early life and education ==
Skinner was born in [[Newton, Massachusetts]] in 1950<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Mantel |first=Linda H. |date=1999 |title=Contributions of Dorothy M. Skinner to the Development of Crustacean Biology |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3884427 |journal=American Zoologist |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=465–470 |doi=10.1093/icb/39.3.465 |issn=0003-1569 |jstor=3884427}}</ref> and went on the graduate from [[Watertown High School (Massachusetts)|Watertown Highschool]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Mykles |first1=Donald |last2=Mantel |first2=Linda H. |date=2005-07-01 |title=Dorothy M. Skinner (1930–2005) |url=https://academic.oup.com/jcb/article/25/3/529/2670541 |journal=Journal of Crustacean Biology |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=529–532 |doi=10.1651/0278-0372(2005)025[0529:DMS]2.0.CO;2 |issn=0278-0372|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Following graduation, she attended [[Tufts University]] where she earned her B.A. in biology and chemistry in 1952.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=April 1, 1996 |title=ORNL affiliate researcher chosen to first fellows of AWIS {{!}} ORNL |url=https://www.ornl.gov/news/ornl-affiliate-researcher-chosen-first-fellows-awis |access-date=2024-05-15 |website=www.ornl.gov}}</ref> In her junior year, she was elected to [[Phi Beta Kappa]]. She was also appointed as the Assistant Dean of Admissions at Tufts and was given the responsibility for admitting two classes to the School of Arts and Sciences.<ref name=":0" />

Skinner participated in the 1953 experimental marine zoology class at the [[Marine Biological Laboratory]], and would go on to serve as an assistant to the class for two more years.<ref name=":2" /> She continued to [[Harvard University]] where she obtained her Ph.D. in 1958 working on [[Bermuda land crab]]s with [[John Welsh (biologist)|John Welsh]].<ref name=":2" />

== Career ==
Skinner conducted post-doctoral research at [[Yale University]] and [[Brandeis University]],<ref name=":2" /> and then moved to the [[New York University Grossman School of Medicine|New York University School of Medicine]] in 1962.<ref name=":2" /> There, she assumed the role of an assistant professor within the Physiology and Biophysics department.<ref name=":0" /> In 1966, Skinner began her career as a fellow within the biology division of [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]],<ref name=":0" /> and by 1978 she promoted to senior research scientist.<ref name=":1" />

== Research ==
Skinner is recognized within the marine research community for her contributions to the development of crustacean biology. In 1962, Skinners's dissertation research resulted in a fundamental publication on the structure and metabolism of ''Gecarcinus lateralis'' integument during different phases of the intermolt cycle.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Skinner |first=Dorothy M. |date=1962 |title=The Structure and Metabolism of a Crustacean Integumentary Tissue during a Molt Cycle |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.2307/1539584 |journal=The Biological Bulletin |language=en |volume=123 |issue=3 |pages=635–647 |doi=10.2307/1539584 |jstor=1539584 |issn=0006-3185}}</ref> In 1975, Skinner made significant points in understanding a crucial aspect of crustacean biology how their muscles break down before they molt, or shed their shells.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yamaoka |first1=Larry H. |last2=Skinner |first2=Dorothy M. |date=1975-12-15 |title=Cytolytic enzymes in relation to the breakdown of the chelae muscle of the land crab, Gecarcinus lateralis |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0305049175902242 |journal=Comparative Biochemistry and Physiology Part B: Comparative Biochemistry |volume=52 |issue=4 |pages=499–502 |doi=10.1016/0305-0491(75)90224-2 |pmid=1204333 |issn=0305-0491|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Her collaboration with Don Mykles started in 1979, and their research highlighted the intricate mechanisms behind muscle atrophy, highlighting the role of specific enzymes and proteins in this physiological transformation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mykles |first1=Donald L. |last2=Skinner |first2=Dorothy M. |date=1981-06-01 |title=Preferential loss of thin filaments during molt-induced atrophy in crab claw muscle |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022532081800883 |journal=Journal of Ultrastructure Research |volume=75 |issue=3 |pages=314–325 |doi=10.1016/S0022-5320(81)80088-3 |pmid=7196959 |issn=0022-5320|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Her review of crustacean regeneration has been recognized as a key summary of the research in the field.<ref>{{Cite book |editor-last=Dinsmore |editor-first=Charles E. |title=A History of Regeneration Research: Milestones in the Evolution of a Science |date=2007-12-03 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-04796-8 |language=en |first1=Dorothy M. |last1=Skinner|first2=John S.|last2=Cook|pages=7–24|chapter=New limbs for old: some highlights in the history of regeneration}}</ref>

== Death ==
Skinner died on February 12, 2005, from complications of Parkinson's disease.<ref name=":0" />

== Awards and honors ==
In 1987 the [[American Society for Cell Biology]] honored Skinner with their Sandra K. Masur Senior Leadership Award.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sandra K. Masur Senior Leadership Award |url=https://www.ascb.org/award/sandra-k-masur-senior-leadership-award/ |access-date=2024-05-28 |website=ASCB |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1993 Skinner received the Award for Excellence in Research from The Crustacean Society.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Crustacean Society Excellence Research Award |url=https://www.thecrustaceansociety.org/TCERA.php |access-date=2024-05-28 |website=The Crustacean Society}}</ref> In 1996 Skinner was elected to the inaugural class of fellows for the [[Association for Women in Science]].<ref name=":1" /> In 1998 there was a [[festschrift]] held in her honor at the annual meeting of the [[Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology]].<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bern |first=Howard A. |date=1999 |title=A Tribute to Dorothy Skinner: A Complete Person |url=https://academic.oup.com/icb/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/icb/39.3.610 |journal=American Zoologist |language=en |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=610–611 |doi=10.1093/icb/39.3.610 |issn=0003-1569|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Personal life ==
On July 24, 1965, she married John Cook, a mammalian physiologist. Together, they had no children.
